title: Slow-cooker split pea soup
subtitle: A thick, warming soup that cooks itself overnight
excerpt: Green split peas and smoked lardons simmered all day with carrot and onion. The peas dissolve into a thick, comforting soup that needs nothing alongside but bread.
sourceNotes: Split pea soup is a classic of Northern European home cooking, common in Britain, the Netherlands, and Scandinavia. The slow-cooker method requires no soaking and no attention during cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. The soup thickens on freezing. Add a splash of water when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Excellent batch-cook soup. Makes 6 generous portions and keeps in the fridge for 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before. The soup thickens as it sits in the fridge. Add a splash of stock when reheating.

content.text: Green split peas do not need soaking before going into the slow cooker. They dissolve almost completely over a long cook and turn the liquid into a thick, smooth soup with very little effort. Do not use whole dried peas here; they need soaking and a much longer cook time.
Smoked lardons add flavour and a little body. If you want to make the soup vegetarian, leave them out and use vegetable stock. The soup is still very good; it just lacks the smoky backdrop.
Serve with crusty bread or toast. A swirl of cream or soured cream in each bowl looks good and softens the flavour slightly.

Rinse {{split-peas-green}} of green split peas and tip into the slow cooker. Add {{lardons}} of smoked lardons, {{onion}} diced onion, {{carrot}} of diced carrot, {{celery}} of sliced celery, and {{garlic}} of crushed garlic. Tuck in {{bay-leaves}} of bay and {{thyme}} of thyme. Pour over {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper-ground}} of black pepper.

Set the slow cooker to LOW and cook for 7 to 8 hours. The peas will dissolve into the broth and the soup will be thick. Discard the bay and thyme. Stir well and taste. Add more salt if needed. Serve as is or use a hand blender for a smoother texture.

rows.symptom: The peas are still grainy after 8 hours
rows.cause: Some older split peas can take longer than expected. The slow cooker may also be running cooler than usual.
rows.fix: Switch to HIGH for a further hour. Add a splash of water if the soup has become very thick. Stir regularly on HIGH.

rows.symptom: The soup is too thick to ladle
rows.cause: The split peas dissolved fully and absorbed most of the liquid.
rows.fix: Stir in 200 to 400ml of hot water or stock until you reach the consistency you want. Taste and re-season after adding liquid.

rows.cause: The peas had less starch than expected, or the slow cooker ran too hot and the liquid reduced a lot.
rows.fix: Cook on HIGH with the lid off for 30 minutes. Alternatively, blend half the soup and stir it back in to thicken.

rows.symptom: The flavour is flat despite the smoked lardons
rows.cause: The lardons may have been mild-smoked or the stock was weak.
rows.fix: Add a teaspoon of smoked paprika at the end and a good grind of black pepper. A squeeze of lemon juice will also sharpen the flavour.

content.text: Split pea soup is a staple of cold-climate home cooking. In Britain it is a traditional winter dish, often made with leftover ham after Christmas. In the Netherlands, erwtensoep is so thick that a spoon is said to stand upright in it. The slow cooker makes this one of the least demanding soups you can produce.
